oneSentence: Some values that should be present in a dataset are absent, leaving blanks that can distort analysis and model behaviour.
plainExplanation:
A dataset is a collection of information organised so people or software can analyse it. Sometimes some entries are missing. A survey may have no age for one person. A clinic record may have no follow-up date. A spreadsheet may have blank cells because the information was never collected, was lost, or could not be matched.

What goes in is incomplete data. What happens next depends on how those gaps are handled. People may remove incomplete rows, fill in a value based on other information, add a special marker such as “unknown”, or redesign the analysis so it can cope with blanks. Each choice changes the result in a different way.

What comes out can be useful, misleading, or unfair. If the missing values are random, the damage may be small. If they are concentrated in one group, place, language, or time period, the output can become biased. For example, if rural areas have more missing health records, a summary may understate their needs.

This is different from noisy data. Noisy data contains values that are present but wrong, inconsistent, or hard to interpret. Missing data means the value is absent. It is also different from class imbalance, where some categories have far fewer examples than others even if the records are complete.

everydayAnalogy.title: Checking a shipping manifest against a delivery
everydayAnalogy.story: A warehouse worker in Mombasa checks a shipping manifest against the boxes that arrived. Some lines on the manifest have the item name and quantity, but the destination shelf is blank. On other lines, the quantity is blank because a label was torn off during transport. The supervisor can still process the delivery, but must decide whether to set those boxes aside, mark them as unknown, or infer the missing detail from other documents. If too many blanks affect one supplier, the stock report at the end of the day may give a distorted picture.

mapping.analogyElement: setting boxes aside or marking unknown
mapping.aiElement: dropping incomplete records or encoding a missing marker
estimating missing values from other available data

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A manifest usually has a fixed set of boxes and fields, while real datasets can have many variables and more complex patterns of missingness. Also, in data work, filling a gap can change statistical relationships in subtle ways; a warehouse guess mainly affects one shipment record. The analogy helps with the idea of blanks and handling choices, but not with the mathematics of bias or uncertainty.

visual.title: How missing data changes results
visual.learningObjective: Show how missing values enter a dataset, the main handling choices, and why different choices can change the final result.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four boxes. It starts with a small table containing blank cells, then moves to a check for where gaps occur, then splits into handling choices, then ends with different possible outputs. Read from left to right to see that the same incomplete input can lead to different results depending on how the gaps are treated.

steps.label: 1. Incomplete data enters
steps.explanation: The dataset includes records with one or more empty values, such as a missing age, location, or date.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a simple table with 4 rows and 4 columns. Leave several cells blank and highlight them with a dashed outline. Add a caption: 'Some values are absent'.

steps.label: 2. Check the pattern
steps.explanation: Ask whether the gaps are scattered randomly or concentrated in one group, source, language, region, or time period.
steps.visualInstruction: Show the same table with coloured circles around blanks. Add small labels above groups of rows such as 'urban' and 'rural' to show blanks clustering more in one group.

steps.label: 3. Choose a handling method
steps.explanation: Common choices are to remove incomplete records, keep them with an 'unknown' marker, or estimate the missing value from other data.
steps.visualInstruction: Split the flow into three side-by-side boxes labelled 'drop rows', 'mark unknown', and 'estimate value'. Use arrows from the checked table to each box.

steps.label: 4. Compare outputs
steps.explanation: Each handling choice can change totals, averages, and model behaviour. The safest option depends on the purpose and the risks.
steps.visualInstruction: Merge to a final panel with three mini-results: different averages, different counts, and a note that one group may now be under-represented. Add a warning icon with text: 'Choice affects outcome'.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each handling method to highlight one possible path from incomplete data to output and reveal a short note on the trade-off.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram explains that missing data is not only about blank cells but about how those blanks are handled. First, a table contains several empty cells. Second, the viewer checks whether the blanks are random or clustered in a particular group, such as one region having more gaps. Third, the process branches into three handling methods: dropping incomplete rows, marking the value as unknown, or estimating a value from other available information. Fourth, the branches lead to different outputs, showing that totals, averages, and model behaviour can change depending on the choice. The core message is that the same incomplete dataset can produce different results because handling missing values is an analytical decision.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Show the same four stages as a static left-to-right diagram with the three handling choices displayed side by side and a fixed note that different choices lead to different outputs.

workedExample.scenario: Before progress report clearance, a programme officer in a country office reviews completion rates submitted by 10 implementing partners.
process: The officer identifies 2 missing values among the 10 expected returns.
Dropping those records gives an available-case average of 71.25% across the 8 reported values.
The tracking log shows that both blanks concern partners that requested workplan extensions. The officer therefore cannot safely assume the values are missing completely at random.

The officer requests the missing returns and checks sensitivity rather than filling the blanks without evidence. If each missing value could range from 0% to 100%, the overall average could range from 57% to 77%.
workedExample.result: The progress report labels 71.25% as an available-case estimate, not the completion rate for all partners. It also records the follow-up and notes that the estimate may be too high if delayed partners had lower completion.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: At the annual workplan review, a legal officer in a regional bureau checks the results framework before the progress report goes to the front office. Several country-office entries show a review deadline but no completion status.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The blank statuses cluster in files returned for revision, so the officer cannot safely assume they are random or count them as completed. Checking the pattern, consulting the tracking log and following up with focal points prevents the progress report from overstating delivery.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not treat blanks as zero, completed or unchanged without evidence, and do not ask an AI tool to invent the missing status. Confidential or case-specific material must not be uploaded to a tool that has not been approved for it. Use approved systems and record any imputation or exclusion clearly.

whyItMatters:
Missing data can quietly change conclusions. A chart, average, risk score, or model may look precise even when important values are absent. For non-specialists, this matters because decisions about funding, staffing, outreach, protection, or evaluation may rest on those outputs.

The key question is not only how much data is missing, but who or what is missing. If gaps are concentrated in one population, language group, location, or period, the result can be systematically unfair or inaccurate. Good decisions require asking whether the blanks are harmless, informative, or a sign that the collection process itself needs attention.
whereYouMayHearIt: At an annual workplan review, when indicator fields are still blank
During progress report clearance, when totals do not reconcile with partner returns
In an evaluation office meeting on whether to impute unanswered survey items
At a vendor demo for a dashboard that quietly excludes incomplete records
During an internal audit review of gaps in administrative records

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Blank cells are just a minor cleaning issue and can usually be ignored.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Sometimes they can be minor, but not always. If the missing values are concentrated in a particular group or type of case, ignoring them can shift averages, hide needs, or make a model perform worse for that group. The impact depends on the pattern, not only the number of blanks.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The best fix is always to delete any row with a missing value.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Deleting incomplete rows is simple, but it can remove a large share of data and can bias the result if the missingness is not random. In some cases, keeping an 'unknown' category or using a suitable estimation method is safer. The right choice depends on purpose, risk, and how the gaps arose.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Missing data and noisy data mean the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They are different problems. Missing data means a value is absent. Noisy data means a value is present but may be wrong, inconsistent, or imprecise. A blank age and an age typed as 250 both create problems, but they need different checks and remedies.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Some information that should be in the dataset is missing, and that can change what the analysis or model produces.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Missing data refers to absent values for variables intended to be observed. Handling it requires examining the pattern and mechanism of missingness. Data are missing completely at random when missingness is unrelated to observed or missing values. They are missing at random when, given observed data, missingness does not depend on the missing values. Otherwise, missingness may be not at random. Treatments include complete-case analysis, missing indicators, imputation, and models that accommodate missingness. The choice affects variance, bias, representativeness, and model performance.

keyTakeaway: A blank is not neutral. Check what is missing and why before deleting, flagging or estimating values, because the pattern can bias the result.

quickCheck.question: Why can missing data be more serious than it first appears?
options: Because blank values always make a dataset unusable.
Because missing values may be concentrated in certain groups and change the result.
Because software automatically replaces blanks with correct values.
Because missing data only matters for very large AI models.
quickCheck.explanation: Missing data becomes especially risky when the gaps are systematic rather than random. If one group has more missing records, summaries and models can undercount or misrepresent that group. A dataset with blanks can still be usable, but only after checking the pattern and choosing a suitable handling method.

issues.problem: The descriptions of missingness mechanisms are technically misleading. “Related to observed variables” does not by itself define missing at random. The key condition is that, after accounting for observed data, missingness does not depend on the missing values. “Related to unobserved factors” is also too loose to define missing not at random.
issues.fix: Missing data refers to absent values for variables intended to be observed. Handling it requires examining the pattern and mechanism of missingness. Data are missing completely at random when missingness is unrelated to observed or missing values. They are missing at random when, given observed data, missingness does not depend on the missing values. Otherwise, missingness may be not at random. Treatments include complete-case analysis, missing indicators, imputation, and models that accommodate missingness. The choice affects variance, bias, representativeness, and model performance.

issues.problem: The marked second option is correct, but the distractors make it obvious without testing understanding. Option 0 is false because blanks do not always make data unusable. Option 1 is the only defensible answer. Option 2 is plainly false because software does not automatically supply correct values. Option 3 is plainly false because missing data matters beyond large AI models. Replace the implausible absolutes with misconceptions that require learners to distinguish missingness pattern, noisy data, and deletion effects.
issues.fix: Replace the options with: ["Because every blank value creates the same amount of bias.", "Because missing values may be concentrated in certain groups and change the result.", "Because missing values show that the recorded values are noisy.", "Because deleting incomplete rows restores the original group balance."] Keep correctOptionIndex as 1.

voicePass.note: The workplace and worked examples now use distinct named roles, artefacts and decision points, while preserving the distinction between available-case analysis and potentially non-random missingness.
